stemBlocks.value: In the diagram O, M and N lie on a straight line with M the midpoint of ON, and P is a point above the line with OP = r and PM = s. (a)(i) Sketch the diagram and insert X on OM such that OX = (1/3)OM. (ii) Produce PX to Q such that PX = 4XQ. (b) Write in terms of r and s: (i) OM, (ii) PX, (iii) QM. (c) Show that PN = 2PM + OP.
Think first: Only two vectors are given, r along OP and s along PM, so build the position vector of every other point out of those two before answering anything.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p286-q09 from workbook page 286.

solutionSteps.instruction: For the sketch, mark X on OM one third of the way from O to M, and extend the line from P through X to Q so that XQ is a quarter of PX.

contentBlocks.value: OX : XM = 1 : 2, and Q lies beyond X on the same straight line as P and X
Result: X and Q correctly placed on the sketch

solutionSteps.instruction: Travel from O to M through P.
Find OX, then PX by going P → O → X.
Find XQ as a quarter of PX, then add it to OX to reach Q.
Subtract OQ from OM to obtain QM.
For part (c), use the fact that M is the midpoint of ON, so MN = OM = r + s.

contentBlocks.value: PN = PM + MN = s + (r + s) = r + 2s, while 2PM + OP = 2s + r
Result: PN = r + 2s = 2PM + OP, as required

strategyBlocks.value: Get OM = r + s from the route O → P → M, place X one third of the way along OM, extend PX by a quarter of its length to reach Q, and use MN = OM to prove the result in (c).

whyThisWorks.value: Because M is the midpoint of ON, the vector MN is identical to OM — same length, same direction — which is what makes part (c) collapse so neatly. Everything else is built by nose-to-tail addition: a route from one point to another can pass through any points whose vectors you already know, and the middle letters cancel. Splitting a segment in a ratio just means taking that fraction of the whole vector, and 'producing' a line means continuing in the same direction, so XQ keeps the direction of PX.

commonErrors.misconception: Treating OM as r or as s alone instead of the sum r + s.
